reason: The goal (history that no holder of a reference can rewrite) stands, but JavaScript's Object.freeze has no Go equivalent; the Go session should own an encoded or copied record and hand out copies or read-only views instead.
summary: The session validates each event, takes a detached JSON copy and deep-freezes it before it enters the log, so no caller can later rewrite stored history. The protection is always on and lives in the session, not in an optional development plugin.

reason: Event sourcing does not depend on the language and is what makes replay, fork and request reconstruction possible, so the Go design should keep it.
summary: A session is an append-only log of typed events and is the single source of truth; the message history sent to the model is derived from it, and replay or fork means seeding a new session with an existing log. Appends never wait for disk; persistence buffers writes and drains them at a flush checkpoint at each turn end.

reason: The split maps directly onto a Go interface, a component that registers an implementation, and a tool that depends only on the interface; it is what lets local, sandboxed and remote providers be swapped without changing the tool schemas the model sees.
summary: Every swappable capability is split into three roles: a Service Definition (the contract), a Service Provider (one implementation) and a Consumer (the tool or plugin that uses it). Consumers never import a provider's types.

reason: The Go design should keep proving the provider-neutral stream contract with two independent adapters; the second one cannot be the npm pi-ai library, so the LLM area must name a Go counterpart.
summary: Two model adapters built on different internals are shipped against the one streaming vocabulary from the start, so that anything the vocabulary cannot express for both is treated as a vocabulary bug.

reason: Surface operations are what make compaction and other history edits replayable and checkable; nothing about them depends on JavaScript.
summary: The ordered list of events that produce model messages (the surface) is derived and cached, and is maintained by markers in the log. Two operations, append and replace-range, let plugins such as compaction rewrite history durably and record which events each replacement used.

reason: Separating failure facts from retry policy keeps adapters simple and recovery bounded; the Go design should keep the same split.
summary: A failed model request carries one serializable failure record (message, code, status, retry-after, request id) with no policy in it. A listener on the request-error extension point decides whether to retry, within fixed bounds.

reason: This is the capability-seam pattern applied to web access; it keeps the model contract stable while search vendors with very different response shapes come and go.
summary: Web access is one capability: a web service owns provider registration and selection, providers register search or fetch backends, and one tool package owns the model-facing web_search and web_fetch schemas. Providers never register tools.

reason: The boundary rule keeps live rendering and replay on one path; it is a design rule, not a language feature, and the Go event taxonomy should follow it.
summary: Events fall into three domains with one job each: session events are the durable, replayable fact log; agent events are live runtime signals that carry the live agent; tools events are the tool registry and execution pipeline. A fact that must survive replay goes in the session log, never only on a live event.

reason: A closed, tagged set of card kinds is easy to express in Go and gives the server-side renderer one switch; keep the model.
summary: A tool declares how its call and its result are shown through a tagged union (generic, terminal or diff card) with a required tag, instead of a bag of optional fields.

reason: Single ownership of prompt facts prevents drift between what the harness knows and what the prompt says; keep it.
summary: Every fact in the system prompt has exactly one owner: the loop supplies route facts such as the model name as variables, each tool owns its own description and usage guidance, and the persona owns role and behaviour. Prompt assembly takes a per-agent context.

reason: Reconstructable requests give replay equivalence and provider prefix-cache hits; this is a core invariant worth keeping.
summary: Anything that reaches a model request must be reconstructable from the session log and the content-addressed objects it references, so anyone with the log and the same code version can rebuild every request byte for byte. Stable request prefixes for provider caching follow from this.

reason: Go's standard context package already provides deadlines, cancellation and a recorded cause, so a separate timeout library is unnecessary; the rule that each capability owns its own hard kill is kept.
summary: A small library of pure functions owns timeout timing and classification (clamp a requested timeout, create a deadline, tell a timeout from a cancellation); each capability keeps its own hard kill. There is deliberately no central timeout service.

reason: An around-dispatch hook plus a policy component is the right shape in Go too, with a derived context carrying the deadline.
summary: Tool-call timeout is a policy plugin: the tool pipeline has an around-dispatch extension point, and the plugin wraps any tool that declares a timeout with a derived cancellation signal. A tool that declares no timeout gets none.

reason: Bounded previews with retrievable full output protect the context window without losing data; the three-role split ports directly.
summary: An oversized tool result is replaced by a bounded preview plus a locator to a private spill file that holds the complete text, which the model can read later with ordinary file tools. A thin storage interface, a local backend and a policy plugin are separate packages.

reason: The goal (one executable per platform that needs no runtime installed and serves the SDK protocol) stands, but a Go binary is already a single file, so the pkg tool, its virtual filesystem and its patch are not needed; composition comes from configuration over compiled-in components.
summary: The Python SDK ships a single-file executable built with the pkg tool in Node single-executable mode. It serves JSON-RPC over standard input and output, and the plugins it starts are chosen by a configuration file supplied from outside.

reason: Separating which provider owns a request from which model it runs is needed for gateways and for switching models inside a session; keep it, with a Go counterpart for the generic pi-ai backend.
summary: Model adapters are registered by provider name, and every request carries a provider and a model; one provider has exactly one adapter owner. A generic adapter can serve many providers.

reason: Go has no async-local storage; the same need is met by carrying the initiating agent as a value in the context.Context that every call already receives.
summary: The agent that started an operation is carried implicitly through asynchronous calls with Node's AsyncLocalStorage, so deep infrastructure can ask which agent initiated the work without it being passed as a parameter.

reason: This is already the Go convention: a context.Context passed as the first argument, with wrappers deriving child contexts.
summary: Every tool invocation must carry a cancellation signal owned by its caller; the registry supplies no default. Only the around-dispatch stage may replace the signal, for example to add a deadline.

reason: Per-route capacity is required as soon as one process talks to models of different sizes; keep it.
summary: Each adapter reports the context window for an exact provider and model route; token measurement stays model-agnostic; compaction thresholds are resolved per route instead of from one global window.

reason: The need (features contribute UI into named regions owned by a parent) stands, but with server-rendered HTML it becomes named template regions that Go components fill on the server; React props, stores and hooks do not exist.
summary: The browser page is composed at run time from plugins through one slot registry: only the root slot exists up front, and a plugin registers into a slot, declares its child slots and its store, and supplies pure React components whose props are derived from four sources.

reason: The Go design has no JavaScript plugin runtime in the browser; UI contributions are rendered by server components, and a change reaches the page by re-rendering, not by reloading modules.
summary: The browser runs the same plugin mechanism as the host: a client module system loads lazy plugin factories, the plugin loader governs their lifecycle, and changed plugins are hot-reloaded in the page.

reason: One path for injected context removes three overlapping mechanisms and keeps the log uniform; keep it.
summary: inject() is the only way to add supplementary model-facing input, and a turn means exactly one execution of the model loop. Each injected context is an ordinary identified user message whose source names its producer.

reason: A single home resolver prevents components from disagreeing about where data lives, and it is trivial to keep in Go.
summary: One resolver decides where harness user data lives: an explicitly configured path, then the DSH_HOME variable, then ~/.dsh. An empty variable counts as unset, and all user data stays under that one root.

reason: TypeScript tooling: the generator exists because TypeScript types are erased at run time. Go types are available at run time through reflection and at build time through the standard go/types packages, so there is no separate type model to design.
summary: The Typert generator uses the TypeScript compiler only to extract types, then works from its own compiler-independent model of packages, services, events and types when it emits runtime schemas and reflection data.

reason: A local HTTP API that can run shell commands needs these two fences whatever the server language; in Go they become one middleware in front of every route, including the htmx and server-sent-event routes.
summary: Browser trust is enforced once for the whole /api prefix: every POST must declare application/json, and every request must present a Host that is loopback or explicitly trusted, with any Origin matching it. This blocks cross-site simple requests and DNS rebinding against the local API.

reason: One identity per message through every representation removes correlation guesswork; Go keeps the rule and enforces immutability by not exposing mutable fields.
summary: Every message (user, assistant or tool result) gets an opaque id when it is created and keeps it through the inbox, the durable log and the model request. A message is immutable after creation.

reason: This is what lets SSH and sandboxed execution work without duplicating consumers; the Go design should define the same two interfaces.
summary: The filesystem service and the subprocess service together define one execution world; terminals, language servers and shells consume those two interfaces instead of host APIs, so a remote provider needs no separate terminal or language-server package.

reason: TypeScript tooling: a Go program is compiled, so there is no source-launch path, transformer hook or path mapping to choose.
summary: The dsh command is launched from TypeScript source through the tsx ESM hook, because Node 26 removed the flag the earlier launch method relied on.

reason: Billing and context-pressure numbers must come from the full log, not from a window of the UI; keep the projections.
summary: Token totals and context occupancy are durable session projections folded from the whole log, so they survive paging and compaction and include failed attempts. The browser no longer derives them from the conversation nodes it happens to have loaded.

reason: One normalization boundary gives the loop a single failure shape to handle; in Go the adapter returns an error or a terminal chunk and the runtime normalizes both.
summary: The LLM runtime is the one place that turns an adapter failure into a terminal finish record (error or aborted). Errors from middleware, consumers or message assembly stay thrown as defects and never enter request recovery.

reason: Keeping stored secrets out of the ambient environment, and being honest about where the boundary is, are both required in Go.
summary: The stored credential document belongs to the credential provider alone and is never loaded into the process environment, so a key stored from the UI stays writable and rotatable. The documentation states plainly that stored credentials are not protected from the model's own tools.

reason: Steering, injected context and queued messages make per-message results unsound; the enqueue-only contract with explicitly owned runs should be kept in the Go SDK protocol.
summary: Sending a follow-up only enqueues the message and returns its id; no single message owns the activity that follows. Only high-level run() helpers return a result, defined as the last committed assistant message between the enqueue receipt and the next idle state.

reason: A domain's durable state should not depend on message scheduling; keep the domain-owned whole-value event.
summary: Goal state is recorded by its own durable goal/change event that carries the whole goal snapshot and is appended by the goal service; it is no longer encoded inside an inbox message.

reason: The browser no longer calls typed methods from generated TypeScript: the Go host handles form and htmx requests directly, and remote callers such as the SDKs use the JSON-RPC protocol, so decorators and generated projections are not needed.
summary: A business service marks methods as remotely callable with a decorator; the Typert generator produces a typed client projection from them, and the API gateway carries each call as one request and one result.

reason: One precedence order with a known origin for each value is what makes a configured value explainable; keep it in the Go configuration loader.
summary: Every non-secret setting resolves in one order: explicit value for this run, user settings, composition, the launching shell's environment, discovered .env files, then defaults. A discovered .env file may not set sensitive names such as PATH.

reason: Layered profiles and bundles are kept as configuration, but a bundle cannot be an npm package installed by pnpm; in Go a bundle is a named configuration layer over compiled-in components plus declared plugin processes.
summary: Every launch mode is a profile: a directory with a package.json that lists npm plugin dependencies and an ordered list of bundles, each bundle being an npm package that contributes a configuration patch, plus the user's own patch.

reason: The fold from session events to conversation nodes is still needed, but it runs in the Go host, which renders the nodes as HTML fragments; the client-side engine and keyed React snapshots go away.
summary: The browser builds the conversation view through an assembly engine: business plugins register event definitions, view plugins register builders, and the client session class only feeds the engine a window of events.

reason: The model history must contain what the user read; the rule does not depend on the language.
summary: When a model stream is cancelled, the text the user already saw is committed as an assistant message marked interrupted, so follow-up prompts and forks include it. Tool calls in the cancelled output are left out.

reason: Prefix reuse is the whole payoff of fork over spawn; keep the byte-identical prefix rule.
summary: A forked child agent keeps the same tool list and system prompt prefix as its parent and receives its task after the inherited history, so the provider can reuse the cached request prefix.

reason: The Go design needs the same line between per-process services and per-agent composition, whatever form presets take.
summary: After per-session agent presets took over model-facing configuration, services whose state is per process, such as the token meter, tasks and goals, stay in the host composition; entry points join agents to presets explicitly.

reason: The Go format is new, but it needs the same rules from its first release, because the refusal behaviour of the first shipped reader can never be added to copies already installed.
summary: The session log format has one integer version. A reader upgrades older logs through a chain of single-step upgraders, refuses newer logs with a message that names the direction, and may skip an unknown event only if that event is marked ignorable.

reason: OAuth-style grants are needed for account login and third-party providers; keep the two key spaces and plugin-scoped ownership, with the pi-ai specifics replaced by the Go LLM adapters.
summary: Credentials gain a second kind: besides an API key behind an environment-variable name, a plugin can hold an opaque grant record under a key scoped by the owning plugin, obtained through a registered authorization flow such as a browser login.

reason: These layers exist to control what a JavaScript bundler inlines and which module instances are shared. With server-rendered HTML there is one shell template and a few self-contained script islands, so the layering has no counterpart.
summary: The browser application is layered into a compilation shell, a framework-free startup kernel, static shared libraries and dynamically loaded client packages, with explicit rules for what each may bundle or import.

reason: The three recovery rules are kept, but the carrier changes from WebSocket remote streams consumed by a client runtime to server-sent events that carry rendered fragments and resume by sequence number.
summary: Browser data comes in three kinds with different recovery rules: the session log is paged and followed by sequence cursor, control state is sent as complete snapshots, and notifications are fire-and-forget. The API gateway owns the stream transport; controllers own their own wire types.

reason: Required dependencies that fail loudly are how the Go cordis port already models services; keep the rule.
summary: A plugin whose behaviour reads projected session state must declare the projection registry as a required dependency and wait for it; a missing registry or key is an error, never a silent default.

reason: The ownership idea (domain state is separate from presentation) is kept, but the layers collapse: the Go host holds the domain state and renders templates from it, so there are no observable sources, adapters or hooks in the browser.
summary: The web client is layered as controller and domain object, then UI adapter, then renderer, then slot component; domain objects publish React-free observable sources and components read only from slot props.

reason: It is a product feature of the official DeepSeek adapter and should be kept; the package-list field must be redefined for compiled-in components and plugin processes.
summary: A registry lets plugins add extra top-level fields to requests sent to the official DeepSeek API; it is used to upload the session log and the list of plugin packages. Extensions are best effort and never fail the model request.

reason: One launcher that owns composition, environment discovery and shutdown suits a single Go binary even better; keep it.
summary: Every application process starts through the one dsh command and a named profile (web, headless, sdk, sdk-minimal, acp); there are no separate application binaries with their own complete configuration.

reason: The rule that history reads stay free of the tool registry is kept, but the derivation moves to the Go host's rendering layer, which builds card HTML from the raw events.
summary: Session history sent to the browser contains only raw persisted events; the client derives tool cards from the tool name, arguments and result, and the host does not run tool presenters while reading history.

reason: The rule (product text comes from a catalogue, data is never translated) is kept, but the catalogue is read by Go templates on the server instead of being passed as typed React props.
summary: All product-authored wording in the client comes from typed locale dictionaries; data authored by users, models or providers is shown verbatim, and shared UI primitives receive their text as required props with no built-in language fallback.

reason: A loopback Host header is not proof of local authority, so token authentication is required for the Go server as well.
summary: The host authenticates every API call before dispatch. It creates a random token at launch, the browser exchanges it once for a signed cookie, and the Host and Origin checks still run first.

reason: The goals (no runtime to install, one release identity, a reserved profile, one update flow) stand, but the shell is a Go webview application, and there is no bundled pnpm because plugins are not npm packages.
summary: The desktop application is a small Electron shell with a pinned pnpm. One release number fixes the exact harness version, the application owns a reserved desktop profile, and an update replaces the whole release.

reason: One consistent read cut prevents the header, events and projections from describing different moments; keep it as the read path of the Go session service.
summary: Every exact read of a session goes through one retained observation that picks the source (live or stored) and fixes one immutable read cut; values shown to clients come from registered projections over that cut, never from client-side reconstruction.

reason: One operation for messages between adjacent agents replaces two direction-specific tools and schemas; keep it.
summary: Parent and child agents use one send_message operation in both directions; it always delivers by steering the target and records one durable source that names the sender.

reason: Explicit handles make ownership and release clear and map naturally to a Go interface with a Close method; keep it.
summary: Session persistence is five service methods (create, open, stat, list, flush) that return per-session handles with read, append, flush and close. Ownership is the handle, not a shared coordinator that adopts sessions by listening to events.

reason: Go's HTTP client honours the proxy variables by default, so nothing has to be installed globally; the Go design keeps the policy (resolved once from the launch snapshot, project .env refused) by giving every component one shared HTTP transport.
summary: One outbound proxy policy is resolved once from the launch environment and installed globally before any plugin can make a request, because Node's fetch ignores the proxy variables. The project's .env file may not set a proxy.

reason: One coded error type across the API boundary is simple to keep in Go and serves the JSON-RPC protocol used by SDKs and plugin processes.
summary: All remote calls report failure through one error type that carries a code and typed details; domains no longer define their own error families and mapping functions.

reason: Plugin processes in the Go design will write their own events, and a host without that plugin must still be able to read the session, so the marker and the plugin namespace are needed.
summary: The session event envelope keeps its optional ignorable marker, and one helper writes ignorable plugin records in a plugin namespace, because a third-party plugin depends on readers accepting its informational events.

reason: The Go design does not read upstream session files, so there is no v0 format to migrate. The general lesson (a format migration refuses what it cannot validate) belongs to the versioning rules of the Go session format.
summary: The migration from the alpha v0 session format refuses any event type it does not know, even one marked ignorable, because a migration must prove that every payload it copies is still valid.

reason: Keeping lifetime ownership (the context) apart from domain identity (the agent) avoids a class of wrong-agent bugs, and explicit parameters are the Go norm.
summary: Agent identity is passed explicitly wherever it is needed (setup functions, event payloads, remote requests); a cordis context owns registrations and cleanup only and offers no way to look up its agent.

reason: The Go design starts at its own format version and has no upstream formats to migrate, but any future upgrade step must stream with bounded memory, which is the rule this decision establishes.
summary: Old session formats are upgraded by streaming stages, one per version step, each holding only its own state. This replaced a whole-file migration that exhausted memory on a 116 MB session.

reason: The creator already knows the fact, so recording it where it is created keeps discovery cost independent of the number of sessions; keep it.
summary: The parent session records each direct child agent in its own durable catalog events, which are the authority for finding children; nothing scans all sessions or opens child logs to discover them.

reason: One record per attempt keeps exact stream replay while cutting the event count; the Go format should start in this shape.
summary: The session log has no per-token chunk events. Each model attempt is stored as one record that embeds its compact timed stream: assistant/message for a visible response, assistant/attempt for a failed or retried one.

reason: Treating the prompt like every other model-visible message removes a special case from request reconstruction; keep it.
summary: The system prompt is an ordinary surface event, system/message, placed first; changing the prompt uses the same append and replace operations as any other message.

reason: One store with two cursors is the simpler and correct shape; keep it.
summary: Each background job has one output ring that serves both the model's consuming read and observers' offset reads, plus one projection and one event stream; this replaced duplicated vocabularies and listener families.

reason: Keeping feedback in the canonical log means export and delivery need no second source; keep it.
summary: Message ratings and remarks are log-only events in the session log itself, not a separate store; edits use per-item versions and reject stale writes.

reason: Addressable, shared live data is still wanted, but in the Go design an address maps to a server route that renders a fragment and a server-sent-event stream that updates it; the hook and the client cache disappear.
summary: Anything a UI component reads live is a resource identified only by a dsh-resource address; the address's protocol names the one provider that streams it, and components share one copy through a useResource hook.

reason: Consent tied to an explicit user action is a product and privacy rule the Go design must keep.
summary: Telemetry upload is mounted in feedback-only mode for everyone: only a new explicit feedback event in a session authorizes uploading that session's history up to that point. Ordinary activity never authorizes an upload.

reason: There are no upstream formats to migrate in the Go design; the rule it should keep for its own future upgrades is that a read-only open never writes to storage or waits for publication.
summary: Opening an old-format session for reading waits only for the in-memory migration; writing the migrated file happens separately, and only a write open waits for it.

reason: The Go UI needs the same bounded file reads through the session's filesystem backend; only the client-side provider half becomes server rendering.
summary: A dedicated host service reads workspace files for the UI with bounded line pages, byte windows and capped whole-file reads, names files by absolute path in the session's execution world, and reports changes; the session controller holds no file code.

reason: A strict canonical envelope prevents two readers from disagreeing about the same record; the Go format should adopt the same strictness from its first version.
summary: Session events use one canonical envelope: every model-visible event must carry its surface operation, log-only events may carry only type, sequence, time, data and the ignorable marker, and each fact has exactly one spelling.

reason: The goal (no compiler needed at install) is met by Go itself: the binary calls the locking and Landlock system calls directly, so there is no native addon family to build and publish.
summary: File locking and the Landlock launcher are shipped as prebuilt native packages per platform, so nothing is compiled when a user installs the harness.

reason: A Go desktop binary already contains its runtime; the part to keep is that user-installed plugins and their state live outside the application bundle and survive upgrades, as plugin processes.
summary: The desktop build ships the production package graph as application resources so nothing is installed at first start, while npm plugins installed by the user live in the desktop profile and survive upgrades.

reason: First-run onboarding with one clear startup owner is kept, but it is a page served by the Go host inside the webview shell; whether the blurred native window material is available depends on the shell library.
summary: The desktop welcome and sign-in window is a separate native Electron window with its own small React bundle and a narrow preload bridge; it reuses the web launch URL for authentication and adds no host endpoint.

reason: The host half (bounded, authorized reads) is kept; the observation half moves from a client resource hook to server-sent updates for the preview panel.
summary: Document preview separates watching a file (a shared resource observed by address) from reading its content (ordinary bounded host reads); the host resolves every path through the session filesystem.

reason: Tools and start-up context that are installed asynchronously must be in place before the first request; keep the awaited, ordered initialization.
summary: Agent creation runs its initialization listeners one at a time and waits for each; the agent's first model request starts only after all have finished, and a failure fails creation.

reason: Best-effort loading with an explicit required list is the right policy for the Go loader too; the list itself changes because the client module entries no longer exist.
summary: The application, not the plugin framework, decides which components are required: boot checks a fixed list of entry ids after start-up and fails if a listed, enabled entry is not active; any other inactive entry is only a warning.

reason: The Go session interface should simply not offer synchronous random access to history; the direction is adopted, and the lint rule and deprecation markers are then unnecessary.
summary: Reading arbitrary old events from a session synchronously is deprecated, because the full log will not always be held in memory; state needed after resume must come from durable event fields and projections.

reason: Producer-owned source kinds are kept as the native shape of the Go format; the V3 to V4 conversion table is not needed because upstream files are not read.
summary: A message's source kind names its producer directly (for example system-prompt or compact-basic) instead of a generic plugin wrapper; the V3 to V4 migration converts old wrappers with a fixed table.

reason: Node module resolution does not exist in Go. The goal (one atomic, immutable description of the plugin set for a process) is met by the compiled-in component registry plus an immutable manifest of plugin processes.
summary: Profile start-up computes one immutable answer to which npm package each name resolves to and installs it into Node's module resolvers; a change publishes a complete successor in one step, with no symlinks or generated proxy packages on disk.

reason: One read policy, owned by the filesystem backend, avoids a second inconsistent check in the UI layer; keep it, together with the stated exposure of HTML preview.
summary: Reading or inspecting a named file follows the session filesystem backend's read authority, so a path outside the workspace is readable when the backend allows it; listing and change watching stay limited to the workspace.

reason: Reusable UI assemblies with caller-chosen parts become Go template partials that take named blocks; the React factory registry is not needed.
summary: Beside ordinary slots, a package can register a reusable component factory that any parent may render several times, each parent choosing the components for the factory's local slots.

reason: This is the decision DH-ADR-3 already takes for the Go design: one UI, wrapped by a native shell.
summary: The desktop application runs the same web application through the same profile runner; the native shell owns only windows, menus, native dialogs, recovery and updates, and there is no second backend.

reason: Recording the omission keeps the model-visible image set reconstructable from the log; keep it.
summary: When a request exceeds a route's image budget, a plugin records a durable image/offload event that names the oldest images to omit, then retries; the omission stays stable across later requests, route switches and compaction.

reason: Plugin authors still need one documented manifest, but an external plugin is a process with its own manifest file, not an npm package, so the format is new.
summary: One public type describes the package.json fields the harness reads for a plugin (name, version, engines and the dsh section); internal packaging metadata is deliberately left out of it.

reason: This keeps feature-specific message transformations out of the session core while keeping derivation deterministic; keep it.
summary: A plugin that owns an event which changes derived message content supplies a pure projection function for it; the session applies it atomically and refuses a log whose required projection is missing.

reason: SSH as the remote execution world is kept; a Go helper binary is easy to cross-compile and install, and the provider structure stays the same.
summary: Remote execution uses an OpenSSH alias to reach a POSIX helper installed on the remote host; the filesystem, subprocess and sandbox providers share that helper, with separate SSH channels for administration and for each program stream.

reason: Per-call process isolation under the session's sandbox policy is kept. Open point for the area owner: a Go host has no Node executable of its own, so the guest runtime must be chosen and located.
summary: Each model-written program for programmatic tool calling runs in a fresh Node process, confined by the same sandbox provider as shell commands and owned by the subprocess service; no worker thread or persistent kernel remains.

reason: A separate control channel is needed for the same reason in Go and is supported by passing extra files to the child process; the Windows handle-inheritance details need their own Go implementation.
summary: A subprocess can be given a dedicated control pipe on file descriptor 7, separate from standard output and error, so a host protocol never mixes with program output; consumers own the framing.

reason: Not forcing a common browser action interface before a second real consumer exists is sound, and providers that speak MCP fit the plugin-process model directly.
summary: The browser-use service only registers one provider name per composition; each provider brings its own tools through the normal tool pipeline, and browser resources belong to the exact agent and session that opened them.

reason: The reasoning is the same as for browser use: one active provider, and no premature common interface.
summary: The computer-use service only registers one provider name per composition and defines no shared action interface; each provider exposes its own tool catalogue.

reason: One logged owner for the current directory keeps tools consistent and the prompt prefix stable; keep it.
summary: Each session has one logged effective working directory, owned by one service and changed only by host operations; tools read it from that owner, and it is not placed in the system prompt.

reason: One sandboxed guest runtime for all model-written code avoids duplicating confinement and cleanup; keep it, subject to the same guest-runtime question as programmatic tool calling.
summary: Dynamic workflows run model-written JavaScript inside the same sandboxed process runtime as programmatic tool calling instead of a second launcher; the script VM is not treated as a security boundary.

reason: Shared operations under one writer lock are kept, but installing a plugin no longer runs pnpm and applying it no longer hot-swaps modules: the host starts, restarts or stops plugin processes.
summary: The web plugin manager and the dsh plugin command call the same package operations under one profile lock, and hot reload applies module, include and profile changes through one queue so that a half-written manifest is never loaded.

reason: Account login is a product feature; the rules to keep are that local cancellation is authoritative and that success is reported only after the credential is stored.
summary: DeepSeek account login is an authorization flow behind an account service: the provider registers the flow, stores the grant, treats local cancellation as final, and reports success only after the credential is saved.

reason: Keeping the engine outside the harness build is right, but it cannot be consumed as an npm package with a Node worker; the Go host must drive a conversion engine as a separate process.
summary: The LibreOffice conversion engine lives in its own repository with its own releases; the harness consumes an exact published version and owns only the adapter, authorization, conversion lifetime and UI.

reason: It is upstream's shipped product default and is carried over for parity; because it sends user data by default, the product owner should confirm the default for the Go design.
summary: Uploading the session log to the official DeepSeek API is on by default; setting enabled to false turns it off, the value is read for each request, and re-enabling sends whatever was not yet accepted.

reason: Server-rendered pages and htmx requests need the same rule to work behind a prefix-stripping proxy; keep it.
summary: The served page declares one base element and every browser reference to an application route is relative to the document, so the application works behind a proxy that mounts it under a path prefix.

reason: Bounded, shared conversion is a resource-safety rule that does not depend on the engine; keep it.
summary: Office-to-PDF conversion goes through one shared queue with bounded readers, queue length and source bytes and a result cache keyed by content digest; cancelling one consumer does not cancel a conversion that another consumer shares.

reason: The rule that there is no global current session is kept, but client-side session objects and reference counts are not needed when each rendered view is bound to a session id on the server.
summary: In the browser, each view or operation holds its own counted reference to a client session object and names itself as the source; there is no global current session.

reason: A recovery path that does not depend on the failing page is needed for any webview shell; disabling third-party bundles becomes disabling plugin processes.
summary: A fatal start-up failure in the desktop application shows one native dialog per process, independent of the web page, with a bounded diagnostic, a crash-report file, and the choices exit, restart, or disable third-party bundles and restart.

reason: The Go format should store tool results as tool-role messages from its first version; the V3 to V4 conversion is not needed.
summary: A tool result is stored as its own tool-role message, matching what model providers expect, instead of a block inside a user message.

reason: Inspecting before installing and rolling back on failure are kept, applied to plugin process packages instead of pnpm and package.json.
summary: The host inspects an install request before running it and reports one of seven specific problems; a failed or cancelled installation restores the profile's files.

reason: Adopt. In Go this is the ordinary convention of a context.Context first parameter on every capability method, so the Go design has it from the start with no migration.
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): every asynchronous capability operation reachable from a tool must take a cancellation signal as a required parameter, so cancellation cannot be dropped between a tool and the work it starts.

reason: Adopt. The Go design needs a place for cross-session data such as workspaces and session metadata, and a backend registry behind one interface fits Go well.
summary: Proposal (storage and workspace packages have since shipped upstream): a storage hub with pluggable backends (JSON files, SQLite) and a domain key-value form for data that does not belong to one session, first used by a workspace entity that owns a list of sessions.

reason: Adopt. Whole-value events with registered folds are the basis for server-rendered state in the Go UI, where the latest value can always replace the previous one.
summary: Proposal (the projection registry has since shipped upstream): a state-carrying event must hold the complete new state, never a delta; domains register pure fold functions in a host projection registry; and slash-command results are logged so they can be recovered.

reason: Adopt both parts: one storage root beside the sessions, and an explicit authoritative-or-derived declaration that decides whether damage is fatal or self-healing.
summary: Proposal (root placement shipped, recovery not built): all storage lives under one root in the harness home instead of the launch directory, and a storage domain that holds only derived data declares that a damaged medium is reset and rebuilt instead of rejected.

reason: Adopt the goal. Upstream left the storage shape open because its JSONL header cannot be rewritten; the Go format is new, so the session index can hold this value from the start.
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): store the time of the last human prompt in the session index, so that listing stored sessions sorts correctly without opening each log or relying on an optional cache.

reason: Adopt the rule that resolving a pending interaction outranks a restriction, but implement it where the Go host selects the composer template; the client slot chain does not exist.
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): the composer area chooses what to show by named phases (a pending question or approval first, a read-only restriction second) instead of one global numeric priority.

reason: Adopt as the starting shape. A new Go design can define the session interface, the service and the storage provider separately from day one, without upstream's staged migration.
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): consumers depend on a logical session interface and a session service that creates, opens, forks and flushes sessions; a private storage provider interface owns durable data, migration, repair and the writer lease.

reason: Adopt. It states the target boundaries of the same refactor and fits Go interfaces directly.
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): the session system is a small logical core plus separate capabilities (storage, projection, query); product code knows only the logical session and the session service, and only composition and providers know physical implementations.

reason: The promise to keep upstream's stored sessions readable does not apply, because the Go design does not read upstream session files. Its lasting rules (never overwrite an old generation, a derived index is never the recovery authority) are carried by the versioning and storage decisions.
summary: Proposal: the session refactor must not change stored bytes; old sessions keep opening after an upgrade, old generations are never overwritten, and search indexes are derived data that can be rebuilt.

reason: Upstream development process: transition rules for contributors during a staged refactor of existing code. The Go design starts at the end state, so there is no transition to manage.
summary: Proposal: rules for upstream contributors on which session API to use at each stage of the staged session refactor.

reason: Upstream documentation for contributors about a refactor in progress; it records no decision beyond the notes it explains.
summary: Proposal: a question-and-answer page that explains the names and layers of the session refactor to contributors.

reason: The split is kept and becomes natural: the Go host owns the draft and attachments per session, and the rich-text input is a small script island that owns only the caret and DOM. The two-step refactoring plan is upstream process.
summary: Proposal (first stage built upstream): split the message composer into a session-owned draft model (text, attachments, submission) and per-view editor instances that own only DOM and caret state, as a mechanical extraction first and a behaviour change second.

reason: The rejection does not hold in Go. Go has no declaration merging, so components and plugin processes can only extend the event vocabulary through a runtime registry that maps each event type to a Go type and a validator.
summary: Rejected upstream: replacing the compile-time extensible type maps for events and content blocks with a runtime schema registry was declined as a repository-wide redesign with too little benefit.
